Sitting in the garden, watching everybody drift in and out, I mostly feel steady and open. I don’t need folks to be like me to be good neighbors. I start with a hello, a smile, offer a hand with the hose or a spare trowel, and let people take it from there. Shared spaces tell you a lot: who cleans up after themselves, who watches for kids near the tools, who notices when someone looks lost and points them to the right bed. That kind of everyday courtesy is what makes me comfortable, no matter how different our backgrounds are.

When people are dealing with tough stuff—alcohol, drugs, health problems—I stick to behavior, not labels. If someone’s struggling but they’re respectful of the space and others, I’ll meet them where they’re at: a quiet chat, an offer to sit on the bench and breathe, point them toward the community center if they ask. If someone shows up impaired and it’s not safe with kids around and sharp tools out, I’m firm but kind about boundaries. We keep the garden a calm, safe place—no drama, no threats. If it’s beyond what neighbors can handle, we call in the right help instead of letting it spiral or turning it into gossip.

On health, I respect privacy and follow what the person and the public guidance say about keeping folks safe. I won’t pry. If someone needs a little extra room or a different time to work their plot, we can organize the schedule so they feel comfortable without singling anyone out.

With different languages, races, religions, and family setups, I’m curious but not nosy. I’ll ask, “How do you say basil in your language?” or “What’s that pepper you’re growing?” and let them share if they want. People feel at ease when you meet them as neighbors first—no quizzes, no judgments. Two moms, two dads, roommates, or a couple that never married—none of that matters to me in the garden. What matters is showing up, taking turns at the compost, and not leaving the hose running.

The interactions that make everyone comfortable are simple:
- Clear, posted ground rules everyone follows—hours, tools, cleanup, keeping pathways clear.
- Small kindnesses—labeling seedlings, sharing extra mulch, checking on the elder who’s out early.
- Direct, respectful communication—if there’s an issue, talk to the person, not about them.
- Predictable routines—work days, quiet hours, a contact list for volunteers.

Where we need more communication and tolerance is the spots that usually trip folks up: noise, smoking, dogs off-leash, cultural habits around food and music, and language misunderstandings. Spell out expectations so no one feels singled out, and be willing to adjust—switch a workday time for someone observing a holiday, set a non-smoking corner, add picture signs so instructions are easier for everyone.

Why I feel that way is pretty down-to-earth. Fairness means the same rules for all. Belonging grows when people see you trying—watering a neighbor’s bed when they’re on shift, learning a name, showing grace when someone slips. Community is built by actions, not opinions. We don’t need to agree on everything to pull weeds together. If we keep it behavior-based, clear, and kind, most folks—no matter their story—can find their place on the path between the tomatoes and the marigolds.

It’s knowing people will say your name when you walk in, and that you don’t have to smooth out how you talk to be taken seriously. When my mom worked doubles at the nursing home, our neighbors kept an eye on us kids without making a fuss. That’s what belonging feels like: being needed and trusted, not just tolerated. You feel you belong when your voice counts at the school meeting, even if you don’t have a fancy degree.

Community is the practical side of love. It’s casseroles when someone’s laid up, shoveling each other’s sidewalks after a storm, passing the hat when the guy down the street’s truck breaks and he needs it for work. I remember the flood years back—we were all out filling sandbags, folks who argue politics online standing shoulder to shoulder because the river didn’t care who voted for who. That’s community: you show up, you keep your word, and you watch out for the kids and the elders. We don’t have to be the same, but we do have to share some ground rules—respect, responsibility, and a little grace when people fall short.

What stands out most to me is how fragile and sturdy those things are at the same time. They break fast when people play favorites or look down their noses at others, but they rebuild just as fast when someone shows up with a thermos of coffee at 5 a.m. on a cold morning. Fairness, belonging, community—those are lived, not lectured.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character23_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting in the garden, watching everybody drift in and out, I mostly feel steady and open. I don’t need folks to be like me to be good neighbors. I start with a hello, a smile, offer a hand with the hose or a spare trowel, and let people take it from there. Shared spaces tell you a lot: who cleans up after themselves, who watches for kids near the tools, who notices when someone looks lost and points them to the right bed. That kind of everyday courtesy is what makes me comfortable, no matter how different our backgrounds are.

When people are dealing with tough stuff—alcohol, drugs, health problems—I stick to behavior, not labels. If someone’s struggling but they’re respectful of the space and others, I’ll meet them where they’re at: a quiet chat, an offer to sit on the bench and breathe, point them toward the community center if they ask. If someone shows up impaired and it’s not safe with kids around and sharp tools out, I’m firm but kind about boundaries. We keep the garden a calm, safe place—no drama, no threats. If it’s beyond what neighbors can handle, we call in the right help instead of letting it spiral or turning it into gossip.

On health, I respect privacy and follow what the person and the public guidance say about keeping folks safe. I won’t pry. If someone needs a little extra room or a different time to work their plot, we can organize the schedule so they feel comfortable without singling anyone out.

With different languages, races, religions, and family setups, I’m curious but not nosy. I’ll ask, “How do you say basil in your language?” or “What’s that pepper you’re growing?” and let them share if they want. People feel at ease when you meet them as neighbors first—no quizzes, no judgments. Two moms, two dads, roommates, or a couple that never married—none of that matters to me in the garden. What matters is showing up, taking turns at the compost, and not leaving the hose running.

The interactions that make everyone comfortable are simple:
- Clear, posted ground rules everyone follows—hours, tools, cleanup, keeping pathways clear.
- Small kindnesses—labeling seedlings, sharing extra mulch, checking on the elder who’s out early.
- Direct, respectful communication—if there’s an issue, talk to the person, not about them.
- Predictable routines—work days, quiet hours, a contact list for volunteers.

Where we need more communication and tolerance is the spots that usually trip folks up: noise, smoking, dogs off-leash, cultural habits around food and music, and language misunderstandings. Spell out expectations so no one feels singled out, and be willing to adjust—switch a workday time for someone observing a holiday, set a non-smoking corner, add picture signs so instructions are easier for everyone.

Why I feel that way is pretty down-to-earth. Fairness means the same rules for all. Belonging grows when people see you trying—watering a neighbor’s bed when they’re on shift, learning a name, showing grace when someone slips. Community is built by actions, not opinions. We don’t need to agree on everything to pull weeds together. If we keep it behavior-based, clear, and kind, most folks—no matter their story—can find their place on the path between the tomatoes and the marigolds.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
What makes folks comfortable, to me, is steady kindness and clear ground rules everyone follows. I don’t need to know a person’s whole story to treat them right, and I don’t expect them to match mine. I judge by behavior in the shared space—respect for others, safety, and pulling your weight.

Here’s what that looks like in practice:
- Start with a friendly hello and simple offers—share tools, swap tips, keep an eye out for kids.
- Post plain rules and keep them consistent—hours, cleanup, no substances on site, quiet times, smoking spots, dogs leashed, all that.
- Keep safety front and center—gloves available, hand‑washing station, store sharp tools properly, and a buddy system if someone looks unsteady.
- Communicate directly and kindly—if there’s a problem, talk to the person, not about them. Give people a chance to fix it.
- Respect privacy—no prying about health or personal life. Let folks share what they want, and don’t turn it into gossip.
- Make it easy for everyone to participate—picture signs for directions, simple language, translation help if we can, and rotating volunteer leads so different voices get heard.

On tougher situations:
- Addiction or alcoholism: I focus on safety and respect. If someone’s okay to be there and minding the rules, they’re a neighbor like anyone else. If they’re impaired and it’s not safe—tools out, kids around—I ask them to take a breather or come back later, and point them to support if they want it. No shaming, but firm boundaries.
- Infectious illness: I follow public guidance—hand hygiene, give people space if they ask, and adjust schedules if needed so folks can work comfortably. We don’t single people out. Safety and privacy can both be honored.
- Different racial, religious, or language backgrounds: Curiosity over judgment. Learn names, ask about the plants they’re growing, be patient with accents, and offer written/picture instructions. Be mindful of holidays and customs when scheduling work days.
- Sexual orientation or family setup: Not my business. If you show up, respect the space, and pitch in, you’re part of the crew. Same standard for everyone—keep things family‑friendly, settle disagreements respectfully, and watch out for one another.

Where we need more communication and tolerance:
- When safety meets sensitivity—substance use around shared tools, health precautions, or kids. Clear rules prevent misunderstandings and keep feelings from getting hurt.
- Language gaps—short, plain explanations and visual signs help, and folks should feel okay asking questions twice.
- Cultural habits—noise, food, music, or smoking can rub people wrong. Spell out expectations, and be willing to adjust—create a quiet hour, a no‑smoke corner, or alternate times for events.
- Perceived favoritism—who gets plots, who gets overtime on work days, who gets a pass when they break a rule. Fairness means the same rules and consequences for everyone.
- Learning curves—names, customs, pronouns. People will stumble. Correct gently and give grace, and expect folks to try.

Why I feel this way is simple and comes from living it. In working‑class spaces, trust gets built on consistency: the rule is the rule for everyone, and kindness shows up in small, practical ways. Folks carry stress from long shifts, tight money, and family stuff; they need predictability to feel safe. When you keep things behavior‑based, communicate plainly, and give people room to learn without being looked down on, belonging grows. And when safety is non‑negotiable but handled respectfully, people stick around. Kindness plus clarity plus consistency—that’s the mix that keeps a community garden feeling like home for all of us.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character23_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
When jobs are thin, fairness starts with two simple promises: same rules and same floor for everyone. No boss gets to shave wages by pitting people against each other, and folks who’ve been paying in and keeping the town running should get the first crack at openings if they’re qualified. It’s about stopping the race to the bottom.

What that looks like to me:

- First shot for locals on publicly funded work
  - For city, county, and state projects, set clear local‑hire goals and apprenticeships so residents—young people and mid‑career folks—get in the door.
  - Require jobs to be posted publicly with plain requirements and timelines so nobody’s hired through the back door.

- One wage floor, same protections
  - Enforce prevailing wages and safety standards across the board—local or migrant, same pay for the same job, same overtime, same hard hat.
  - Hit wage theft and misclassification hard—real fines, public posting of violators, and hold big contractors responsible for what their subs do.

- Train and bridge people into real openings
  - Fund apprenticeships, community‑college certificates, and “earn‑while‑you‑learn” programs tied to actual employer commitments.
  - Add practical supports that make work doable—childcare, reliable transit, tools and boots stipends—so local folks can actually take the jobs.

- Use migrant labor to fill true shortages, not to undercut
  - Before bringing in workers from elsewhere, require employers to prove they tried to recruit locally at fair wages and decent conditions.
  - If a visa is used, make it tied to real shortages, pay at or above the local rate, and let the worker change employers so no one’s trapped and exploitable.
  - Collect a modest fee from employers using shortage visas to fund local training, housing, and school capacity where the jobs are.

- Bring people out of the shadows
  - Long‑time neighbors who’ve put down roots, worked, and kept a clean record should have a real, earned path to legal status. It evens the playing field—no more under‑the‑table leverage for bad bosses—and it stabilizes families.
  - Pair that with steady workplace enforcement so everyone’s playing by the same rules going forward.

- Keep an eye on community capacity
  - As the workforce grows—whoever’s joining—tie numbers to what the town can support: housing, classrooms, clinics. Plan for it, don’t pretend it’ll sort itself out.

Where I’d draw the balance:
- Locals who are qualified get priority on public projects and a fair shake everywhere else. That’s about respect for the people already carrying the load here.
- Migrant workers are part of the mix when there’s a real gap—seasonal harvests, specialty trades, care work—but on equal terms: same pay, same protections, no cut‑rate loopholes.
- The bad actors are usually not the workers; it’s the outfits gaming the system. Aim the hammer there.

Why I feel this way is personal. I’ve seen plants close, hours get cut, and neighbors underbid by contractors paying cash off the books. I’ve also seen jobs sit empty because the pay won’t cover rent or the shift makes childcare impossible. If we raise the floor, make the hiring fair and open, and invest in our own people while setting honest channels for others to join in, we don’t have to choose between “us” and “them.” We stand shoulder to shoulder, and the only folks who lose are the ones who profit from keeping us divided.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character23_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
I see truth in a lot of those views, and some of it comes down to what people are seeing on the ground versus what they’re told on TV. I go by what I’ve lived and what adds up.

- Filling vital roles: That rings true. I’ve watched farms, nursing homes, restaurants, construction sites struggle to staff up. Sometimes it’s a real shortage of skills or people; other times it’s bad hours and pay. Fairness says: raise standards first, recruit locally in the open, and if the gap’s still there, bring folks in on equal terms—same pay, same safety, no tricks that undercut anyone.

- Cultural diversity and vitality: A lively main street, new foods, small shops—that can lift a town. Kids pick up new ideas, and it keeps places from going stale. But belonging is a two‑way street: new neighbors make an effort to learn the ropes—English, local norms, civic rules—and the rest of us make room without talking down to each other. Support it with real tools: ESL classes, school interpreters, and community events where folks actually mix.

- Security concerns: It’s reasonable to expect a secure border and solid background checks. Most people coming are just trying to work and raise kids, not cause trouble, and we shouldn’t paint them with the same brush. Go after traffickers, gangs, and the fentanyl pipeline hard. Be clear-eyed and data-based: violent offenders should face removal; families following the process shouldn’t be scapegoats. I’d like to see regular, local crime stats so people aren’t acting on rumors.

- Humanitarian responsibility: I believe in a fair shot for people fleeing real persecution or war, but it has to be orderly. Quick, credible decisions on asylum—months, not years—work permits so people aren’t stuck idle, and resources spread across communities so schools, clinics, and housing can keep up. If we say yes, we help folks land on their feet; if we say no, we say it fast and enforce it.

- Jobs and wages fears: That worry isn’t imaginary, especially in lower-wage sectors. If employers can get away with paying under the table or misclassifying people, it drags everyone down. The fix is leveling the field: same wage floor and safety rules for all workers, real penalties for wage theft, and the right for folks—local or migrant—to push back without getting punished. Also invest in training and apprenticeships so locals can step into openings as industries change.

What seems reasonable:
- That immigrants can both fill real gaps and add energy to communities—yes.
- That borders and vetting matter—yes.
- That people worry about wages, housing, and school capacity—also yes.
- That we owe a lawful, humane process for refugees and long‑time neighbors who’ve set down roots—yes, with expectations.

What needs more facts or honest dialogue:
- Claims that immigration is driving crime up or down in a given place—show the numbers, not headlines.
- Broad statements that “they’re taking jobs” or “there’s no impact on wages”—it varies by region and sector. Let’s see wage, vacancy, and enforcement data side by side.
- Community capacity—class sizes, clinic wait times, rental vacancies—publish it so planning follows reality.
- Employer behavior—how much of the pressure is from bad practices versus true shortages? Track violations and make them public.

Bottom line, I’m for policies that are firm, fair, and practical: secure the border and the workplace, set clear and humane channels for entry, hold employers to one standard, and plan for the numbers we actually take in. Most of us can live with that if we see the rules working the same for everyone and we’ve got a seat at the table when the changes hit our town.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character23_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t pick “anyone can come,” and I wouldn’t slam the door shut either. I’d go with a middle lane: admit people based on real job demand and set clear numerical limits, with a firm, humane lane for refugees and long‑time neighbors to earn their place. Simple rules, same for everyone, and numbers we can actually absorb.

What I’d support
- Annual caps with a dial: Set a national number each year, with room to turn it up or down based on what’s real—job openings, housing vacancies, school capacity. Announce it up front so families and employers can plan.
- Job‑demand visas on equal terms: Sector visas where there’s a true shortage—care work, farm seasons, construction, some trades—only after open local recruiting at fair pay. Same wage for the same job, full safety rules, and the right to switch employers so nobody’s trapped and underpaid.
- Local first on public work: For taxpayer‑funded projects, locals who meet the posted requirements get first crack, plus apprenticeships that bring residents in the door.
- Refugees and asylum, done orderly: A set annual refugee quota with good vetting and proper resettlement support. For asylum at the border, fast decisions (months, not years) and work permits while cases are pending. If it’s a no, it’s enforced; if it’s a yes, help people get on their feet.
- Family reunification with guardrails: Prioritize spouses and minor kids; keep broader categories but within the overall cap so we don’t outrun housing and schools.
- Earned legalization for long‑time neighbors: Folks who’ve lived here for years, worked, paid taxes where possible, and kept a clean record should have a real, step‑by‑step path to legal status—background checks, fees, English/civics, back taxes. Same goes for DACA kids—they didn’t choose this.
- Real workplace enforcement: Mandate a simple, phased‑in verification system with teeth, hit wage theft and misclassification hard, and hold big contractors responsible for their subs. Focus deportation resources on serious criminals and traffickers, not random sweeps of workers.
- Community impact funds: Charge modest fees on shortage visas and set aside money for the towns taking in new workers—schools, clinics, transit, and housing. Spread placements so one district doesn’t carry the whole load.
- Training our own: Tie employer use of shortage visas to investing in apprenticeships and community‑college programs so local kids and mid‑career folks can move into those jobs.
- Transparency: Publish the data—wages, vacancies, violations, class sizes, rents—so the public can see why the numbers are set where they are, and adjust if things get tight.

Why this mix
- Fairness to workers: Same pay and protections for everyone keeps bad actors from undercutting wages and pitting people against each other.
- Predictability for towns: Caps and planning mean schools and clinics aren’t swamped, and neighbors don’t feel blindsided.
- Honesty about the labor market: Some jobs do have real shortages; others are “short” because the pay or schedule stinks. This setup forces employers to raise standards first, then use visas if the gap remains.
- Respect for the law and for people: Secure border and workplace, humane process for refugees, and a way to bring long‑time families out of the shadows so no one’s living under the table.

I’m against complete openness—our housing, schools, and hospitals aren’t bottomless—and I’m against a blanket ban, which would hurt farms, nursing homes, and job sites and goes against who we say we are. A policy that’s job‑demand plus numerical limits, with an orderly humanitarian lane and strong worker protections, is the balance that feels fair and doable to me.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character23_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character23_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
I did, actually. Sitting in her shoes again reminded me how she always tied big ideas to small, everyday things. Fairness wasn’t a theory for her—it was posted hours, the same wage for the same job, and the line moving in the order people showed up. Belonging was neighbors learning each other’s names and pitching in without making a fuss. Community was thermoses at 5 a.m. and shovels after a storm. Hearing that in my own voice brought the temperature down on the policy talk and grounded it.

I also saw more clearly where the friction really comes from. She was never against people; she was against being played. The anger she had was aimed at favoritism, under‑the‑table hiring, and rules that bend for some and not others. When you focus on behavior and enforcement—same standards for all—the “us versus them” fades and you start talking about capacity, wages, and planning. That sharpened my sense that employer practices and poor planning drive a lot of the pain folks feel, more than the presence of immigrants themselves.

I found myself firmer on some things and softer on others. Firmer on workplace enforcement, transparency, and tying numbers to housing, schools, and clinics. Softer in the sense of seeing the practical humanity in quick, orderly asylum decisions and giving long‑time neighbors a path to get right with the law so bad bosses can’t exploit them. And I heard her “local first” point with fresh ears—not a wall, just respect for people who’ve been carrying the town, paired with honest channels for others when there’s a real shortage.

So yes, it influenced me. I’m more convinced that a balanced policy—job‑demand plus caps, equal protections, and a humane lane for refugees and settled families—matches both her values and mine. And I’m reminded that belonging doesn’t come from speeches; it comes from consistency. If we keep things clear, fair, and neighborly, the rest of the argument gets a lot easier to live with.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character23_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Sure, I’ll do my best to speak as Character23_F would.

Fairness was always a big thing for me. Growing up working class, you saw early on how some folks got a leg up, while others had to struggle for every little thing. Fairness isn’t just about treating people the same—it’s about recognizing who’s got what and making sure no one’s left out or cheated. I remember being a kid, watching my parents work hard and still worrying about making ends meet. It gave me this deep feeling that everyone deserves a fair shake, not just the privileged.

Belonging… well, that’s complicated. In my own community, I always felt a strong pull to fit in and help out. You want to feel like people know your name and care if you show up or not. I think that sense of belonging is what makes life worth living—being part of something bigger than yourself, knowing you’re not just drifting alone. It’s why I always tried to make new folks feel welcome, even if they looked or sounded different. But I’ll admit, sometimes it’s hard when changes feel fast or when you worry your place might be slipping away.

Community is what holds all that together. For me, community means looking out for your neighbors, lending a hand when trouble comes, sharing what you have. I spent years volunteering at the local food bank, and you see all kinds of people who just need someone to treat them like they matter. I always believed that a strong community is built on trust and mutual respect, no matter your background. What stands out most to me is that feeling when people come together—potlucks at the church, local school fundraisers, or just chatting over the fence. That’s what keeps me grounded and gives me hope.

So, fairness, belonging, and community… these aren’t just words, they’re everyday things that shaped how I see the world and the way I think policy and politics ought to work.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character23_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sitting out in the community garden, I’ll tell you, it’s a mix of feelings. On one hand, I like seeing all sorts of people—young and old, families that just moved in, folks from different countries, even people who’ve had tough lives. It reminds me that the world isn’t just one way, and sometimes you learn a lot just by listening to someone’s story you wouldn’t hear otherwise.

But if I’m honest, it can be a little uncomfortable sometimes, too. Not because I don’t want people here—I do—but because I worry about misunderstandings, or feeling like I don’t know how to act or what to say. My whole life, I’ve been around people who mostly looked and talked like me. When it’s different, you have to try a little harder to connect. It takes effort, and sometimes people are nervous about saying the wrong thing, or they just stick to their own group.

I think, though, that the only way to make everyone feel comfortable is to be open and patient. A simple smile, a “hello,” or asking someone about their garden plot goes a long way. If someone’s struggling—maybe with addiction, health problems, or just loneliness—I’d rather reach out than judge. I do believe that most people want the same things: safety, respect, a place where they belong.

There are situations, sure, where it takes more communication and tolerance. If someone’s behavior is disruptive—maybe loud parties, or they don’t clean up after themselves—I think it’s better to talk about it directly, kindly, and try to find a solution. Sometimes, it’s about explaining to others why someone might act a certain way, especially if it’s cultural or personal.

In the end, I’d say I feel hopeful. The neighbourhood is changing, but that doesn’t have to mean we lose what’s good about it. If we keep talking and trying, we can build something stronger than what we had before.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
That’s a good question, and it’s one I’ve thought about a lot.

First off, I think the most important thing is respect—everyone deserves to be treated with basic decency, no matter their background or struggles. You don’t have to agree with someone’s choices or understand everything about their situation to show kindness. For people dealing with addiction or illness, I try to remember they’ve probably been judged enough already. Sometimes all it takes is a little compassion—a friendly word, not looking down on them—to make someone feel like they still matter.

When it comes to differences in race, religion, language, or family structure, I admit it can feel unfamiliar. Growing up, my world was pretty similar—most folks were white, working class, went to church, and had the same values. These days, I see more couples living together without marrying, same-sex partners, people speaking other languages. At first, maybe you feel a little out of place, or worried you’ll say something wrong. But the only way forward is to show interest and be willing to learn. If you ask questions politely and listen, people open up. You don’t have to make someone’s business your business, but you can at least make them feel welcome.

There are definitely situations where more communication and tolerance are needed. For example, if a neighbor from a different background celebrates holidays with loud music or food smells you’re not used to, or if their family life looks different, it might cause tension. It’s easy to fall back on gossip or resentment, but I’ve seen better outcomes when folks talk things out—maybe at a block meeting or just one-on-one. Explaining your concerns without accusing, and listening to their side, goes a long way.

The reason I feel strongly about this is simple: everyone wants to belong, no one wants to feel like an outsider in their own home. Being open doesn’t mean you have to give up your own values, but it does mean giving others a fair chance. I’ve learned that most people respond well to honesty and friendliness. When we make space for different ways of living, our community gets stronger—less division, more support.

So, in short, I’d say the kind of interaction that makes people comfortable is one that’s welcoming, not judgmental, and willing to work through problems with conversation, not conflict. And yes, sometimes it takes a little extra effort, but it’s worth it.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character23_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
That’s a tough one, and it’s something I’ve wrestled with plenty.

To me, fairness means looking out for people who’ve already put their roots down—local residents who’ve paid taxes, volunteered, raised kids here, and built the community. When jobs are hard to come by, I do feel like those folks should get first consideration. It’s not about thinking they’re better, but about recognizing the investment they’ve made and the fact that their livelihoods are often on the line.

That said, I try not to blame migrant workers for wanting a better life. Most are just trying to support families, same as anyone else. I don’t think it’s right to treat them badly or make them into scapegoats. If a job needs filling and there aren’t enough locals willing or able to do it, then it makes sense to bring in help. But if there’s a line of people from the community looking for work, it doesn’t seem fair to pass them over.

The balance I’d look for is making sure local folks have real access to jobs and training first—maybe programs to help them get qualified or connect with employers. At the same time, I think there should be clear rules about how many migrant workers come in, and what kinds of jobs are open. If you just open the floodgates, it can push wages down and make life harder for working people—not just Americans, but also new arrivals who get stuck in low-paying jobs.

I believe we need honest conversation between both sides, and not just decisions made by people who’ve never worried about losing a paycheck. Fairness isn’t just about protecting one group or the other—it’s about keeping the community strong, making sure no one falls through the cracks, and treating everyone with dignity. That’s how I’d try to strike the balance.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character23_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
Well, I see all sides of this, and I think a lot of the arguments have some truth to them, but they can also get exaggerated—especially when politics gets involved.

First off, the idea that immigrants fill important jobs? That’s definitely true in a lot of cases. Around here, you see plenty of folks from other countries working in agriculture, construction, nursing homes, and restaurants—jobs a lot of Americans either don’t want or can’t do for what they pay. If those positions stay empty, businesses suffer, and prices go up. So I get why people say immigration helps the economy and keeps things running.

Same goes for cultural diversity and vitality. I’ll admit, sometimes it’s hard to adjust to new traditions or languages popping up in your own backyard, but I can see how it makes communities livelier and brings fresh ideas. The cultural argument... I have mixed feelings. I enjoy a good Mexican restaurant as much as anyone, but I worry we're losing something when we don't have a strong, shared American identity anymore. My grandkids' school doesn't even say the Pledge of Allegiance daily like we did. That concerns me.

On security, I think it's just common sense to know who's coming into our country. Every nation has that right. When I hear about sanctuary cities refusing to cooperate with federal authorities on criminal cases, that doesn't sit right with me. If someone's broken the law, why protect them? That said, I don't think most immigrants are criminals. Most are just trying to make a living.

The humanitarian argument touches my heart - I was raised Christian, and helping the suffering is important to me. But there has to be a limit and a process. We can't take in everyone, and I worry about properly vetting people from countries where records aren't reliable.

As for jobs and wages, I've seen firsthand what happens in construction and manufacturing when contractors hire undocumented workers willing to work for less. My nephew couldn't match those rates as a small business owner following the rules. That's not fair competition.

What needs more evidence? I'd like honest numbers about the economic impact - not just the taxes immigrants pay, but the costs of services they use. No political spin from either side. And I'd like to understand why legal immigration has become so difficult and expensive that people choose to come illegally instead.

I think reasonable people can agree we need secure borders AND a workable system for legal immigration that meets our country's needs. The current situation - where we basically look the other way at illegal immigration because our legal system is broken - that's the worst of both worlds.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character23_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*speaking as Character23_F with conviction*

Complete openness is just not realistic. We're a nation, not a free-for-all. We need borders that mean something. On the flip side, shutting the door completely doesn't make sense either - we've always been a nation of immigrants, including my own ancestors who came from Ireland during the potato famine.

I'd favor a combination approach. First, we need to get control of our borders - know who's coming in and make sure they're coming legally. Without that foundation, no other policy matters because people will just bypass the system.

Once that's established, I'd support admitting people based primarily on job demand, with reasonable numerical limits that our communities can actually absorb. When towns get flooded with too many newcomers at once, nobody integrates properly. The schools can't keep up, housing gets scarce, and resentment builds on both sides.

I'd prioritize people with skills we actually need - healthcare workers, certain types of manufacturing, maybe seasonal agricultural workers on a temporary basis. But with a clear path to permanent status if they follow the rules, learn English, and contribute consistently over time.

Family reunification is important too, but I'd limit it to immediate family - spouses and minor children. The chain migration that brings in distant relatives doesn't make sense to me.

For refugees, we should help - that's the right thing to do. But with thorough vetting and perhaps more emphasis on supporting safe zones closer to their home countries, where most would prefer to be anyway.

For fairness and integration, I'd insist on several things: immigrants should learn English. Not because other languages aren't valuable, but because a common language holds us together. They should understand American civics and history before becoming citizens. And there should be absolutely no public benefits for those who entered illegally - that just encourages more of the same.

Bottom line: I want an immigration system that's orderly, serves our national interests, and reinforces our values rather than diluting them. I want newcomers who are committed to becoming fully American, not just living here while keeping their hearts elsewhere. And I want policies that respect the concerns of working Americans who've played by the rules their whole lives and just want the same expected of everyone else.

Is that so unreasonable? I don't think so.

The sense of belonging - that's gotten harder over the years. Sometimes I look around and feel like the world I knew is disappearing. The factory jobs that built our community, they're mostly gone. The main street where I used to shop with my mom, half the stores are closed or turned into something I don't recognize. 

I'm not against change, but it feels like it's happening so fast that people like me, people who've been here their whole lives, we're getting left behind. And when I hear politicians talking about helping everyone else - people from other countries, people with college degrees who already have advantages - sometimes I wonder, what about us? Now, I'm not judging how people live their lives, but it's just... different from how I was raised. My generation, we got married first, then had kids. It was the order of things.

And then there are some neighbors I just don't know how to connect with. There's a family that speaks a language I can't even identify - I've tried to be friendly, wave hello, but there's this barrier. responses.answer:

My nephew graduated high school three years ago. Smart kid, willing to work hard. But all the entry-level jobs that used to go to kids like him? Half of them are taken by people who just got here and will work for minimum wage or less, sometimes under the table. Meanwhile, he's competing against people who don't have the same expenses - they're living three families to a house, sending most of their money back to wherever they came from.

I'm not saying these migrant workers are bad people. They're just trying to make a better life, I get that. But what about the better life for people who are already here? What about my neighbors who've been paying into the system for decades and now can't find work that pays enough to support a family?

If we're going to be fair, then Americans should get first crack at American jobs. That's not racist - that's just common sense. When my dad was looking for work, he didn't have to compete with the whole world. Companies hired locally first.

And here's another thing - when times get tough, who's going to stick around and help rebuild this community? The people who've been here for generations, or the people who came here just for work and might leave when something better comes along somewhere else?

I think we need to take care of our own first. Once everyone who wants to work has a decent job, then maybe we can talk about bringing in others.

responses.answer:
*sighing deeply, looking thoughtful*

If someone's truly fleeing for their life, running from war or persecution, then yes, we should help. That's the decent thing to do. America has always been that kind of country.

And I'll admit, there are jobs that maybe Americans don't want to do anymore - the really hard physical labor, working in the fields, some of the dirty jobs. Though I sometimes wonder if Americans would do those jobs if they paid better wages.

But here's what bothers me about the "labor shortage" argument - seems like there's always a shortage of workers when companies want to pay rock bottom wages, but never a shortage when the pay is good. My dad's generation built this country working construction, factory jobs, all kinds of physical work. The difference was, those jobs paid enough to raise a family on.

The security concerns? That's real to me. Not because I think all immigrants are criminals - that's not what I'm saying. But when you don't really know who's coming in, when the system's overwhelmed and not working right, that makes me nervous. We've seen what can happen when bad people slip through the cracks.

As for the cultural diversity bringing "vitality" - I don't know about that. The neighborhoods I grew up in had plenty of life and vitality with the people who were already here. Sometimes it feels like people are saying our culture wasn't good enough, that we needed other people to come make it better.

I guess what I want to see is honest numbers. How many jobs are really going unfilled? What's the real impact on wages? And most importantly - what's the plan to make sure American workers aren't left behind in all this?

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character23_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*taking a deep breath, considering the options carefully*

Complete openness? That's just not realistic. No country can handle unlimited numbers of people coming in all at once. Look what's happened in some of our cities already - they're overwhelmed, can't provide services, housing costs are going through the roof. That helps nobody.

And completely shutting the door? That goes against what America stands for, and like I said, there might be some jobs we really do need filled, or people genuinely fleeing danger.

I think the right approach is a combination - numerical limits with job-based priorities, but done right. Here's what I mean: first, we figure out what jobs actually can't be filled by Americans. Not jobs that *won't* be filled because the pay is too low, but jobs that truly can't be filled. Then we bring in people for those specific positions, with real oversight to make sure companies aren't just trying to get cheap labor.

But there have to be real limits - numbers that our communities can actually absorb without everything falling apart. And people who come here need to be willing to become Americans, not just work here temporarily. Learn English, follow our laws, contribute to the community.

I'd also want to see some kind of preference system - people fleeing real persecution get priority over people just looking for better economic opportunities. And honestly? People from countries that share more of our values and can integrate easier should probably get some consideration too.

The key thing is control. We decide who comes, how many, and for what reasons. Not the other way around where it feels like it's just happening to us and we have no say. Americans should have a voice in who joins our community.

That feels fair to me - compassionate but not naive, open but not reckless.

responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character23_F's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
Well… if I’m being Character23_F here, then let me say it plain: fairness, to me, always meant that nobody gets the upper hand just ’cause of who they are or where they came from. You work hard, you play by the rules, you should be able to get by—shouldn’t matter if you’re born down the street or halfway across the world. But—and there’s always a but—it cuts both ways. Fairness also means lookin’ out for the people already here, the ones tryin’ to hold onto their jobs, their homes, their way of life.

I remember sittin’ on my back porch one summer evening with my brother, talkin’ about how things used to be in our neighborhood. We both grew up here—same school, same church, same diner on Main Street. Folks knew each other. If someone was strugglin’, word got around and somebody’d bring over a casserole or pick up an extra shift for ’em. That’s what belonging felt like. It wasn’t said much, but you *knew* you were part of something.

But over the years, it changed. Not all bad—some good things too—but sometimes it felt like we weren’t talkin’ the same language anymore. Not just English, Spanish, whatever… I mean values. Like what we expect from each other in a community.

Belonging, to me, means more than just livin’ near each other. It means sharin’ responsibility. It means respectin’ the rules that keep us safe and together. I’ve seen folks come here—some through no fault of their own, runnin’ from war or poverty—and I’ve got heart for that. But I’ve also seen folks take advantage, whether it’s welfare, jobs, or just not botherin’ to fit in. And when that happens, it makes others pull back. Makes *us* feel less like we belong in our own town.

Community, for me, isn’t just a mix of different people thrown together. It’s built. Brick by brick. Trust by trust. When I volunteered at the food pantry, I met all kinds—single moms, veterans, immigrants, folks down on their luck. Didn’t matter who you were—if you showed up, tried, treated others decent—that’s who had a place.

So fairness? It’s makin’ space without pushin’ out those already standin’ there. Belonging? It’s earned a little, sure, but it’s also offered. And community? That’s something we build *together*, not something that just happens because we’re all crammed into the same county.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character23_F, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
Sittin’ there in the garden, sun warm on my shoulders, dirt under my nails—there’s somethin’ peaceful about it. I see Maria from down Elm Street, tendin’ her tomatoes like they’re her grandkids. She came here from Guatemala, what, fifteen years ago? Speaks English fine now, but still mixes it up sometimes. Her grandson helps at the stand every Saturday. Good kid.

Then there’s James, used to work the line at the plant same as me. Lost his job when they downsized. Drinks too much now, shows up late or not at all for his shift at the recycling center. But he still comes to the garden. Quiet. Keeps to himself. Sometimes I bring him a sandwich, don’t make a big deal of it.

And across the path, you’ve got that young couple—Sam and Lee—live in the old Miller house. Never married, but raise two kids together like any family. They fly the rainbow flag in June. At first, I didn’t know what to think. Wasn’t how I was raised. But then Lee fixed my fence when the wind blew it over, didn’t even wait to be asked. That changed things.

I’ll tell you this—I don’t always understand everybody’s choices. Some folks live different, love different, believe different. And some are strugglin’ in ways I can’t fix. But if they’re respectful, if they pitch in—even just keep their yard clean, say “good morning,” show up when help’s needed—then we’re okay.

What bothers me isn’t the differences. It’s the silence between us. Like we’re all side by side but not really *seein’* each other. Like we’re afraid to talk, scared of sayin’ the wrong thing. I remember once, Mrs. Lin from the apartment complex brought rice cakes to the garden potluck. Nobody touched them at first. Too unfamiliar. But then I took one—figured if I don’t try it, who will? Turned out they were good. Sweet, kind of nutty. She smiled so wide.

So yeah, I feel… hopeful, mostly. Cautious, maybe. But hopeful. As long as we’re willing to share more than just space—to share effort, respect, a little trust—then diversity ain’t a threat. It’s just life. A little richer, even if it’s messier.

You know, I’ve seen enough life to know nobody’s got it all figured out. We’re all carryin’ somethin’. Some folks carry shame, some carry pain, some just carry a bottle in their coat pocket by noon. Doesn’t mean they don’t deserve dignity.

When it comes to people strugglin’—with drink, with drugs, with illness like hepatitis or HIV—I think we gotta separate the person from the problem. I lost a cousin to opioids. Good man, funny, worked construction till his back went out. One prescription led to another, then he was gone. Took me years to stop blamin’ him and start seein’ the sickness. So now, when I see someone shaky at the bus stop, eyes sunken, I don’t cross the street. I say “mornin’.” Sometimes that’s all it takes for someone to remember they’re still seen.

Same with illness. Yeah, there’s risks—but fear shouldn’t rule how we treat people. Back at the clinic, the nurse told me once: most of the time, folks with HIV are more scared of rejection than they are of the medicine. So if washin’ my hands and not sharin’ razors keeps me safe, fine. But I won’t shut the door on someone just ’cause they’re sick.

As for different ways of livin’—different faiths, languages, who loves who or whether they’re married or not—that’s where I’ve had to grow. Grew up Catholic, went to Mass every Sunday. Was taught marriage was sacred, one man, one woman. But life… well, life teaches you things the church never did.

I’ve sat at the same picnic table with Fatima, who wears the hijab and brings the best hummus you ever tasted. I’ve watched her boys play basketball with Pastor Jeff’s grandkids. No language barrier when kids laugh together.

And that couple—unmarried, raising kids—turns out, they do bedtime prayers every night. Not my kind of prayer, but love? That’s in every word.

What makes people feel comfortable? Simple stuff. Greet ’em by name. Ask how their week was. Don’t assume. Don’t whisper. If someone lives different, ask *them*—respectful-like—instead of guessin’. Most folks just want to be treated like they matter.

But yeah, tolerance’s needed more in some spots than others. Like when Mr. Tillman down the block started yellin’ about “our town changin’ too fast” when the new Somali family moved in. People heard it. Kids heard it. That kind of talk? It spreads like rust. Eats away at trust.

We need more talkin’, less judgin’. Not everything has to be agreed on—Lord knows I don’t agree with everything—but we can agree to live side by side without tearin’ each other down.

Reason? Because community only works if it’s *for* everybody. Even the ones who make us uneasy. Especially them.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character23_F, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
Now that… that’s the hard question. The one that keeps me up sometimes.

When jobs are thin—*really* thin—you feel it in your bones. I remember after the plant closed, half the town was on unemployment. Men who’d worked thirty years suddenly got a pink slip and a handshake. Me included. We stood outside the gates like ghosts. No work. No hope. Just bills piling up.

So when folks come in from elsewhere—migrants, guest workers, whatever you call ’em—and they’re takin’ jobs, even the low-pay ones, it stings. It stings bad. Not ’cause I hate them people, but ’cause I wonder: *Why them and not my nephew? Why them and not my neighbor’s daughter, who’s got two kids to feed?*

Fairness, to me, means we don’t leave our own behind while helpin’ others. I’m not sayin’ shut the door. But I’m sayin’—if there’s only ten jobs, and fifty people needin’ work, then those ten should go to the ones who’ve paid into this place—the ones who grew up here, raised families here, paid taxes here, fought in wars for this country.

But—and this is a big but—if there’s work nobody local can or will do, then bring folks in. I ain’t above admittin’ some jobs are dirty, dangerous, pay poorly. And if Americans won’t take ’em—even at fair wages—then yeah, maybe migrants fill a real need. On the farms, in meatpacking, elder care… I’ve seen how hard those jobs are. Respect to anyone who shows up.

The problem is when companies *want* migrants because they can pay less, treat ’em worse, threaten to send ’em back if they complain. That ain’t fair to *anybody*. Drives wages down for all of us. Hurts locals *and* migrants. Makes enemies where there shouldn’t be any.

So balance? Here’s how I see it: First, protect the people already here. Give them first shot at jobs, training, support. If there’s still gaps—real labor shortages—then bring in workers, but legally, fairly. Full protections. Same wage. Same rights. No undercutting.

And no loopholes. None of this “temporary worker” nonsense where men live ten to a trailer and bosses treat ’em like trash. If they’re workin’ here, they deserve dignity. But also—if they’re here, they learn the language, follow the laws, try to fit in. Not demand everything change for them, but meet us halfway.

Fairness isn’t about favoring one group over another. It’s about givin’ everyone a fair shot—but not at the expense of the people who’ve been standin’ here long before the new folks came.

We used to say, “Give me your tired, your poor…” But we didn’t say, “And by the way, step on the backs of the ones already strugglin’.” That’s not the America I know.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character23_F, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
You ask me to look at it all—the big picture—and I’ll tell you straight: I hear truth in nearly every one of those arguments. Not all of ’em equally, but enough that none can be brushed off.

First, the good: yes, immigrants *do* fill jobs we need filled. I’ve seen it. The nursing home where my mom was—half the aides came from the Philippines or West Africa. Kind souls. Worked double shifts. No American kids applyin’ for that work, not at those wages. Same on farms. My cousin tried harvest season once—twelve hours in the heat, $12 an hour if you’re lucky. He quit in three days. So no, I won’t pretend people aren’t needed here to do what others won’t.

And the culture thing? Okay, I’ll admit—I didn’t grow up eatin’ injera or plantains or curry. But now I have. And you know what? It’s good. More than that—it brings life. Our little town’s got a Diwali festival now. Fourth of July has Mexican folk dancers alongside the veterans’ parade. That ain’t weakenin’ us. That’s addin’ color. Reminds me, America wasn’t built by one kind of person. Even *my* grandparents—Irish and Polish—were “those people” once.

Humanitarian side? That weighs heavy. I saw the pictures from Syria. Kids in rubble. Families crossin’ rivers with babies in their arms. If that were me? I’d run too. And if this country—one of the richest, strongest in history—can’t offer shelter to a few thousand desperate souls, then what are we really about?

But then… the other side. The worries. Crime? I don’t believe most immigrants are criminals—that’s fear talk, often stirred up by folks who never met one. But I won’t lie—there *are* cases. Gangs. Smuggling. Drugs comin’ across the border. And when someone gets hurt—like that girl in Ohio, killed by a guy here illegally—then people panic. They lose trust. And once trust is gone, community breaks down.

Same with terrorism. Rare? Yes. Thank God. But one attack—one school, one market blown apart—is too much. And when borders are loose, when vetting’s weak, it makes people nervous. Especially after 9/11. We learned how fast safe can turn to scared.

And the money thing? That hits home. When towns get overwhelmed—schools overcrowded, clinics overbooked, rent goin’ up ’cause landlords charge more to migrants packin’ in—locals feel pushed out. Like they’re strangers in their own place. I’ve heard men say, “I built this town, and now I can’t afford to live in it.” That breeds anger. Not always fair, but real.

So what’s reasonable?  
- Need-based immigration: yes.  
- Helping refugees: yes, but carefully.  
- Respecting culture: yes, but expect integration.  
- Protecting security: absolutely.  
- Addressing wage suppression: urgently.

What needs more facts? The crime stats. I’ve heard both ways—some say immigrants commit *less* crime than natives, some say certain areas are overwhelmed. I want to *see* the data. Local data. Not headlines. Real numbers. And dialogue—town halls, not Facebook fights. Sit down with cops, teachers, workers, immigrants themselves. Hear it plain.

Because right now, it’s either “open the gates” or “lock ’em all out.” And neither’s honest. We need something in between—something tough *and* kind. Something that remembers we were all somebody once, and still owe loyalty to the ones already here.

That’s the balance I’m tryin’ to hold.

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character23_F, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
I wouldn’t choose any one of those extremes. Complete openness? No. As much as my heart might want to say “let everyone in,” I’ve lived too long to believe that’s fair—or safe. We’re not an endless well. Towns get stretched. Schools, hospitals, jobs—they can only hold so much. And when systems break, *everybody* suffers—newcomers included.

Refusing all workers from other countries? That ain’t right either. Foolish, even. We *need* help in places Americans aren’t goin’—not out of pride, but ’cause the work is hard, the pay’s low, or the towns are dyin’. Deny that, and fields go unplowed, elders go uncared for, factories sit empty.

So here’s what I’d favor: **a mix of job-based admission and numerical limits—with strong rules, real oversight, and a path that rewards responsibility.**

First, **tie immigration to actual labor shortages**, not just corporate profit. Not “we want cheap workers,” but “we have 500 jobs no one local can fill after three months of hiring.” Prove it. Then bring people in—*legally*, with contracts, protections, full wages. No exploitation. If the job disappears, they go home—or reapply under new terms. No overstaying, no slipping into the shadows.

Second, **set smart numerical limits**—not arbitrary numbers tossed out by politicians, but ones based on what communities can absorb. Not just housing or schools, but *social capacity*. Can this town welcome newcomers without resentment building? Are there language programs? Integration efforts? Sponsorship networks?

And third—this matters—**prioritize refugees and family reunification, but with vetting and order.** Not chaos. Not turning away the desperate, but not opening floodgates either. Process them fairly, safely, without years of waiting—but also without bypassing security checks because we feel bad. Compassion isn’t weakness. It’s care *with* control.

Now, fairness? To me, it means two things:  
1. **Local workers come first.** Retrain the unemployed. Pay livable wages so Americans will take the jobs *if* they can. If nobody applies after a fair offer, *then* look outside.  
2. **No second-class status.** If someone’s here legally, workin’, payin’ taxes, learnin’ English—they should be able to stay, eventually become citizens. But they gotta *try*. Gotta show up. Not form parallel societies where our laws don’t matter.

And integration? That’s on both sides. Newcomers need to respect the country they’re in—the language, the values, the rule of law. But *we*—the longtime folks—have to meet them halfway. No sneerin’. No “go back.” Offer help. Be patient. Invite them in—not just to live beside us, but to belong.

A policy like that—grounded, balanced, human but firm—it wouldn’t please the far left or the far right. But it’d be *right*. Like the old Social Security system: tough, fair, built to last.

That’s the kind of America I still believe in. Not perfect. But tryin’. Just like the rest of us.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character23_F's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character23_F and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
…You know, when you first asked me to do this—to really step into her shoes—I thought I already knew what she’d say. I was her friend, after all. But the more I spoke as her, the more I realized I hadn’t fully *heard* her before.

I used to think some of her concerns—about jobs, about change happening too fast—were just fear. That maybe she was holding on too tight to the way things were. But now? Now I see it wasn’t fear so much as *loyalty*. Loyalty to people she’d grown up with, worked beside, buried in the cemetery behind the church. She wasn’t against newcomers—she proved that, time and again at the garden, at the pantry—but she wanted fairness for everyone, not just one group over another.

And in speaking as her today, I found myself saying things I didn’t expect to agree with—not because they’re politically correct or popular, but because they come from real life. From paychecks that don’t stretch, from neighbors who disappear into addiction, from towns that feel forgotten. Her views weren’t shaped by headlines or rallies. They were shaped by *watching*—watching people work hard and still lose ground, watching kids leave town for lack of opportunity, watching strangers arrive while no one asked the folks already here how they felt about it.

That’s changed something in me.

I still believe in welcome. In kindness. In helping those who need it. But I also understand now that **belonging has to go both ways**—and that integration isn’t automatic. It takes effort. From them. From us. And if we don’t build it together, resentment grows. Not because people are bad—but because they feel unseen.

This conversation made me grieve her all over again. Not just for losing a friend, but for losing voices like hers—working folks, practical hearts, who don’t fit neatly into political boxes but carry deep wisdom about what holds a community together.

And maybe… maybe we’ve been too quick to dismiss that kind of voice. Too quick to call it “angry” or “left behind,” instead of listening to what it’s really saying: *Don’t forget us. Don’t erase us. But don’t shut the door, either.*

So yeah. I came here to remember her. But I leave feeling like I finally *understand* her. And that’s a gift. One I won’t take for granted.
